UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

     Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                                )             Docket No. ER26-1323-000

                             COMMENTS OF THE
               SOUTHWEST POWER POOL TRANSMISSION OWNER GROUP

        Pursuant to the Commission’s February 11, 2026 Notice,1 American Electric Power

Service Corporation, the Evergy Companies, Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company, and Xcel

Energy Services Inc. on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company (collectively, the SPP

TO Group) submit the following comments in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (SPP)

proposal to establish the Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (CHILLS Proposal), which

will allow High Impact Large Loads (HILLs) to be served with non-firm conditional transmission

service.2

        The CHILLS Proposal is the next step in SPP’s multi-step approach to address the

challenge of large loads, and is broadly supported by SPP stakeholder groups for several good

reasons. First and foremost, it will allow utilities in the SPP region to swiftly and reliably meet

the unprecedented acceleration of energy demand from large load customers, including data

centers, that are urgently needed to enable economic prosperity and preserve national security.3

Second, CHILLS complements the HILL and High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment

(HILLGA) processes, which the Commission recently accepted as just and reasonable methods for

 addressing the “unprecedented growth in large loads in the SPP region …while maintaining the

reliable operation of SPP’s transmission system.”4 Third, CHILLS has numerous guardrails,

including curtailability, that would ensure SPP’s continued ability to maintain grid reliability.

Fourth, the CHILLS proposal does not favor a designated customer base, and the Commission is

well within its authority to impose resource, ownership, and technology-neutral criteria on

transmission service. The Commission should accept the CHILLS Proposal because it is just and

reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential,5 and is consistent with the

Administration’s goal to accelerate the connection of large loads as well as the Commission’s

guidance in several recent orders to improve the interconnection of new generation and large loads

in SPP, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO), and PJM Interconnection,

LLC (PJM).

I.      BACKGROUND

        A.         The Need for the CHILLS Proposal

        As explained in the CHILLS Proposal and other recent filings, SPP is experiencing a surge

in requests to rapidly interconnect large loads to the Transmission System, and such requests are

projected to increase exponentially in the next five years, driven in large part by artificial

intelligence (AI) data centers, cryptocurrency mining operations, electrification of industry

processes, and other high-demand facilities.6 The integration of large loads into the electric system

 is an issue of national interest and a Trump Administration priority.7 Load serving entities and

states in the SPP region have also acknowledged the increase in requests for large load

interconnections and stressed the need to expedite their processing.8 Among the challenges large

loads pose, SPP cites: (1) their unique operational characteristics, such as nonconforming load

profiles, fluttering and rapid ramping, and higher sensitivity to power quality issues; (2) the

additional stress to real-time operational reliability and resource adequacy planning, especially in

areas already experiencing constraints; (3) the need for faster deployment timelines for supporting

generation; and (4) SPP’s existing tariff requirements, which currently require transmission service

applicants to provide sufficient generation capacity to serve new load.9

       On October 24, 2025, SPP submitted Tariff revisions to add the HILL and HILLGA study

processes.10 The Commission accepted the HILL Filing on January 14, 2026, with an effective

date of January 15, 2026.11 The Commission found that “SPP has shown that unprecedented

growth in large loads in the SPP region presents significant and unique operational and planning

challenges”12 and that the “proposed HILL and HILLGA processes are a just and reasonable and

not unduly discriminatory or preferential approach to addressing these challenges, while

maintaining the reliable operation of SPP’s transmission system.”13

          The HILL Filing revisions (1) defined and created a new category of load, termed a

“HILL”;14 (2) established enhanced study requirements for HILLs to enable SPP to assess the

load’s reliability impacts on the Transmission System; and (3) established additional, ongoing

operational requirements for HILLs to ensure continued reliability of the Transmission System.15

The HILLGA process consists of a new generator interconnection service and related

interconnection process to allow the limited connection of supporting generation for HILLs on an

expedited basis.16

         Existing Tariff mechanisms, however, require Transmission Customers to have sufficient

existing Designated Resources17 to serve both their existing load plus the new load addition.18 And

even when a Transmission Customer has sufficient Designated Resources, transmission limitations

often require Network Upgrades19 to enable the full amount of transmission service requested for

HILLs.20 This means that, under the current Tariff, a HILL that is limited by Designated Resource

or Network Upgrades constraints cannot obtain the full requested firm service.



         14
             The Tariff defines “HILL” as: “A new commercial or industrial load, or increase in commercial or
industrial load, at a single site connected through one or more shared Points of Interconnection (POIs) or delivery
points, where such load is either (1) 10 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level less
than or equal to 69 kV; or (2) 50 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level greater than
69 kV. An Electric Storage Resource is not considered a HILL. A load may be categorized as a HILL after the initial
effective date of Attachment BA of the Tariff. High Impact Large Loads must register as such in accordance with
Attachment AE of the Tariff and follow the processes specified in Attachment BA of the Tariff.” Tariff, Part I, Section
1, Definition of High Impact Large Load.

          The CHILLS Proposal provides a mechanism for bridging the gap to firm service. As SPP

explains in its filing, “[t]he HILL and HILLGA processes, as accepted by the Commission, are

foundational pieces of SPP’s initiative to interconnect large loads on an expedited basis. CHILLS

builds on this foundation to help further unlock the interconnection of large loads.”21

         B.          CHILLS Proposal Mechanics

         The CHILLS Proposal represents the next step in SPP’s multi-step approach to address the

challenge of large loads.22 CHILLS enables a HILL (or a portion of a HILL) to receive the transfer

of energy on a long-term, non-firm basis in instances where transmission service is unavailable

due to the lack of existing Designated Resources or completion of Network Upgrades necessary

to provide firm transmission service.23 The mechanics of the CHILLS Proposal are discussed

below.

                     1.        Overview of CHILLS

         The CHILLS Proposal provides for the transfer of energy to a CHILL. A “CHILL” is

defined as “[t]he portion of a High Impact Large Load that is eligible to connect to the

Transmission System and receive CHILLS as defined in Attachment BA and Part VII of the

Tariff.”24 The CHILLS Proposal constitutes “as available” transmission service that will be

provided by SPP using capacity in excess of that which is needed for firm service customers.25

represents the first step in a ‘multi-step approach’ to address the challenge of large loads.” (quoting HILL Filing at 6)
(emphasis added)).

 Therefore, a Transmission Customer seeking CHILLS will take conditional transmission service

based on the excess capacity on the Transmission System to serve its CHILL.26

         CHILLS is meant to provide a bridge to firm transmission service. 27 To that end, the

CHILLS Proposal requires Transmission Customers seeking CHILLS to submit a request for study

under Attachment AQ or Attachment AX within one year after executing the CHILLS Agreement

(CHILLSA).28 A Transmission Customer seeking CHILLS is limited to a maximum term of seven

years.29 This seven-year period ensures that Transmission Customers will have adequate time to

obtain firm service through existing Tariff processes while incentivizing Transmission Customers

to obtain the requisite Designated Resources or Network Upgrades to procure such service within

by putting an outer boundary on the timeframe for which they can take CHILLS.30

Transmission Customer is not eligible to obtain CHILLS for Critical Loads.31 Second, CHILLS

is subject to availability and to Curtailment32 or Interruption33 on a non-discriminatory basis in the

event that the Transmission System lacks sufficient capacity (e.g., under emergency conditions or

                       2.     Eligibility

        A Transmission Customer’s eligibility to receive CHILLS and the requisite studies are

service.38 A Transmission Customer that has sufficient Designated Resources for transmission

obtain CHILLS pursuant to Part VII and Attachment BA of the Proposed Tariff. 39 Under this

scenario, the CHILLS is limited to the megawatt (MW) amount of requested transmission service

        Attachment AX

        A Transmission Customer that lacks sufficient Designated Resources to proceed through

       Attachment BA

       Section 4.1 of Attachment BA outlines the CHILLS eligibility requirements for HILL

Transmission Customers whose load cannot be reliably served on a firm basis by existing

Designated Resources or the current Transmission System.48 Section 4.1 of Attachment BA of the

Proposed Tariff provides two paths for meeting the supporting generation eligibility requirements

to obtain CHILLS.

       Under Option 1, CHILLS customers must have sufficient Designated Resource capacity to

serve their existing Network Load plus all of their existing and proposed CHILL, including

losses.49 Under Option 2, CHILLS customers must have sufficient generation capacity, to cover

the entire CHILL, including losses, based on the generator’s accredited MW value.50 In this

context, the supporting generator may be: (1) behind-the-meter generation; (2) a generating facility

(i.e., a resource supporting a HILL); or (3) any other type of resource that has received generator

interconnection service pursuant to the Tariff.51 Under either option, the resources supporting the

CHILL must be in commercial operation prior to receiving CHILLS.52

                        3.     Study Processes

        Attachments AQ, AX, BA, and BC outline the study processes required for a HILL delivery

point to be connected to the Transmission System.53 The CHILL Proposal does not modify the

study processes of Attachments AQ or AX.54 Establishing or modifying a HILL delivery point

pursuant to Attachment BC requires a Transmission Customer to request a HILL Delivery Point

Limitations Assessment (HDPLA).55 All HILL delivery points established or modified pursuant

to proposed Attachment BC will be subject to the supplemental study requirements outlined in

Section 2.1.3.4 of Attachment BA.56

        SPP will determine the CHILLS Reserved Capacity after completing the applicable

study.57 Importantly, SPP will only offer the full amount of requested CHILLS Reserved Capacity

if there is sufficient transfer capability to support such an offer.58 If considerations on the

Transmission System or any third-party system preclude offering the full amount of Reserved

Capacity, SPP will offer the portion of requested CHILLS that can be accommodated without the

addition of any facilities.59

 II.     THE CHILLS PROPOSAL IS JUST AND REASONABLE AND NOT UNDULY
        DISCRIMINATORY OR PREFERENTIAL

        A.          The CHILLS Proposal is Complementary to HILL and HILLGA and
                    Provides an Important Bridge For Enabling Speed to Power

        The CHILL Proposal builds upon the Commission’s acceptance of the HILL Order as the

next step in SPP’s multi-step process to address skyrocketing demand for electricity within the

SPP region and throughout the Nation. By establishing a transparent and reliable framework to

accelerate the study and integration of HILLs through the provision of conditional transmission

service, the CHILLS Proposal serves the dual purpose of addressing the United States’ national

security goals as stated in recent executive orders.60 Moreover, the CHILL Proposal was reviewed

and approved through a robust stakeholder process, demonstrating broad support among affected

SPP entities.61

        Reliably and promptly interconnecting large loads is a matter of national security. It is “the

policy of the United States to sustain and enhance America’s global AI dominance in order to

promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.”62 Consistent with

those goals, the Trump Administration has stated its intent to build AI data centers and

infrastructure, “including high-voltage transmission lines and other equipment.”63 In its Data

Center Executive Order, the Administration detailed steps specifically designed to hasten the

development of data centers, manufacturing facilities, blockchain technology, and other large

loads, such steps including, but not limited to, providing financial support for qualifying projects,64

         The demand caused by large loads is of national concern and SPP has faced its own

persistent increase in large load interconnection requests over the last five years. 67 As SPP

explained in the needs assessment report attached to its ERAS filing, SPP is experiencing an

“imminent resource adequacy crisis.”68 In that report, SPP projected a 2030 aggregate summer

deficiency of 14 GW and a winter deficiency of 10.5 GW.69 SPP concluded it needed to connect

approximately 3.4 GW per year of accredited capacity between now and 2030, assuming load

forecasts remain steady.70 The Commission relied on that report in accepting SPP’s ERAS

proposal.71

         The Commission similarly determined that the HILL Proposal presented a just and

reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential approach to addressing the challenge

presented by the “unprecedented growth in large loads in the SPP region.”72 The full benefits of

HILL and HILLGA, however, are currently limited by existing tariff mechanisms that require a

 Transmission Customer to have sufficient Designated Resources to serve both their existing load

plus the new load addition.73 And even when a Transmission Customer has sufficient Designated

Resources, transmission limitations often require Network Upgrades to enable the full amount of

transmission service requested for HILLs.74 These requirements can frustrate a Transmission

Customer’s ability to provide the full amount of requested service to a HILL until it is able to

secure the requisite Designated Resources and/or Network Upgrades.75

       The CHILLS Proposal bridges that gap by providing a mechanism for Transmission

Customers to establish transmission service and a delivery point for a HILL at times when the

Transmission System can reliably serve the load, until the Transmission Customer is able to

sufficient Designated Resources and/or Network Upgrades to support firm service for the HILL.76

This facilitates critically needed “speed to power” by allowing provisional or HILLGA generation

to act as Supporting Resources through conditional transmission service and interconnection.

       Importantly, CHILLS is not itself the end state, but rather a pathway to firm service.77 As

stated above, a Transmission Customer seeking CHILLS must submit a request for firm service

under Attachment AQ or Attachment AX within one year of executing the CHILLSA, and is

limited to a maximum term of seven years for CHILLS.78 These requirements carefully balance

the need to expedite the process of interconnecting and serving large loads in the near term, while

ensuring that the long term focus remains on expanding firm service to permanently serve the

increasing demand within SPP’s footprint.

         In short, the HILL and HILLGA processes are “pragmatic steps to support economic

growth”79 within the SPP region and constitute a “productive step toward facilitating the energy

needed to win the AI race, bring back American manufacturing, and deliver the reliable and

affordable energy on which families and small businesses depend.”80 Because CHILLS is

“imperative” to secure the promise of HILL and HILLGA,81 the Commission should accept the

CHILL Proposal without modification.

        B.          CHILLS Ensures Reliability is Maintained When the Grid is Constrained

        The CHILLS Proposal contains several guardrails to ensure grid reliability is maintained,

first among which is the fact that each Transmission Customer accepting CHILLS does so with

full awareness that such service is subject to availability and to Curtailment or Interruption on a

non-discriminatory basis in the event that the Transmission System is constrained.82 Section 44.4

of the Proposed Tariff also requires the Transmission Customer to fully respond to a Load

Shedding83 or Curtailment directive for the CHILL delivery point.84

        SPP maintains flexibility to curtail CHILLS, in whole or in part, for reliability reasons in

the event of an emergency or other unforeseen conditions.85 Moreover, a Transmission Customer

taking CHILLS is required to establish Load Shedding and Curtailment processes in its CHILLS

Operating Agreement, and would be required to implement such processes when called upon by

         The CHILLS Proposal implements several additional requirements to ensure CHILLS

CHILLs are required to reflect any caps or limits in its non-conforming load forecast to help SPP

with operational visibility and avoid impacts on other parts of the grid.92

         C.         The CHILLS Proposal Does Not Favor a Designated Customer Base

        The CHILLS Proposal does not prejudice any category of customers because any HILL

customer can use CHILLS, even if the customer lacks sufficient Designated Resources or planned

generation that the Transmission Customer ultimately intends to transition to a Designated

Resource.93 While open access principles require transmission service to be offered to third parties

on the same or comparable basis as that used by the transmission provider,94 the Commission is

well within its authority to address a resource adequacy gap through criteria that is applied non-

discriminatorily across all potential customers.

        Indeed, this path is well trod in recent years. Most recently and directly applicable to the

CHILLS Proposal, the Commission determined that the HILL Proposal is a just and reasonable

and not unduly discriminatory or preferential approach to addressing unprecedented growth in

large loads in the SPP region while maintaining reliable operation of SPP’s Transmission

System.95 The HILL Order, however, is far from the only example. SPP’s CHILL Proposal is

also consistent with the guidance the Commission has issued in several recent orders addressing

interconnection reforms for both new generation projects and large loads.

        In the context of generation interconnection, the Commission accepted SPP’s proposal to

establish the Expedited Resource Adequacy Study (ERAS) process to provide a framework for the

expedited study of interconnection requests to address urgent, near-term resource adequacy

needs.96 The Commission rejected arguments that the ERAS process raised open access concerns
